question: What did the actuary Benjamin Gompertz show in 1825 about human mortality rates over much of adult life?

receipt.quote: In 1825, the actuary Benjamin Gompertz read a paper, ‘On the nature of the function expressive of the law of human mortality, and on a new mode of determining the value of life contingencies’, to the Royal Society in which he showed that over much of the adult human lifespan, age-specific mortality rates increased in an exponential manner.

question: In human populations such as India, Mexico, Sweden and the USA, roughly how long did the mortality doubling time stay after mid-life (age 40)?

receipt.quote: Despite large differences between these populations in the levels of mortality in earlier life, the slopes in a graph of log mortality rate against age showed a close approximation to parallelism after mid-life (40 years), with a mortality doubling time consistently around 8 years.

question: Why is advancing age the major risk factor for cancer, cardiovascular disease and dementia, according to evolutionary reasoning?
answers: Because natural selection has not had an opportunity to maintain fitness at older ages, so older age brings loss of function and chronic disease
Selection has not kept the body fit at ages most people once never reached

receipt.quote: Natural selection has therefore not had an opportunity to maintain evolutionary fitness at older ages. Presumably as a consequence, advancing age is the major risk factor for diverse types of loss of function, and for highly prevalent chronic and killer diseases, including cancer, cardiovascular disease, and dementia [6, 7].

question: What finding about people who live beyond 100 years suggests that illness can in principle be squeezed into the very end of life?
answers: Late-life disability and morbidity are lower among people living beyond 100 years
Centenarians have less late-life disability and illness

receipt.quote: Interestingly, it has been found that late-life disability and morbidity are lower among people living beyond 100 years [18]. Morbidity can thus be restricted, at least in principle, to the very end of life (Fig. 1).
